explanation: SET NOCOUNT OFF sends row-count messages for each statement in this procedure.
XACT_ABORT is OFF even though the procedure opens transactions; some runtime errors can leave a transaction active.
@CustomerIdText fixes the customer lookup to customer '1' instead of using @CustomerID.
@OrderID starts at business identifier 1, which remains the fallback if subsequent assignments find no rows.
SELECT * returns every Sales.Orders column, including three nvarchar(max) columns, and makes the result shape depend on the table schema.
No ordering determines which ten OrderID values are returned.
OrderID is the primary key of Sales.Orders, so DISTINCT cannot remove any rows.
NOLOCK permits the Orders query to return uncommitted data or to miss or duplicate rows during concurrent changes.
YEAR(OrderDate) requires extracting the year rather than comparing OrderDate directly with range boundaries.
The order filter fixes the reporting year at 2016.
Comparing int CustomerID with nvarchar @CustomerIdText requires converting the variable to int; a nonnumeric value would fail.
The predicate must support both all orders and a selective CustomerID lookup, which can make a single cached plan inefficient.
The leading % in '%urgent%' requires a substring search across order comments.
ISNULL wraps indexed Orders.CustomerID unnecessarily: the column is NOT NULL and can be compared directly.
The comparison selects customer 1 regardless of the supplied @CustomerID.
Adding zero to OrderID obscures a direct equality predicate on the primary key.
CustomerID <> 1 can qualify most orders rather than selecting a narrow key range.
Customer 1 is excluded by a fixed business identifier.
TOP (1) chooses an unspecified order/customer pair.
CROSS JOIN pairs orders with customers without requiring the customer to own the order.
No ordering determines which matching order line supplies the returned OrderID.
The comma-separated Orders and OrderLines sources separate their relationship from the FROM clause.
The scalar line count depends on the outer OrderID and can require repeated lookups in Sales.OrderLines.
EXISTS tests OrderLines for each outer OrderID logically; a join to distinct qualifying OrderIDs would preserve the one-row-per-order result.
The qualifying order-line quantity threshold is fixed at 1.
ORDER BY repeats the CASE expression instead of referencing HasComments, so the two definitions can drift.
ORDER BY 2 silently changes meaning if OrderDate moves in the select list.
OrderDate is not unique. Orders sharing a date can change position across page requests without an OrderID tie-breaker.
The first branch selects the fixed OrderID 1.
Each branch selects a different primary-key value, so UNION performs logically unnecessary duplicate elimination.
The second branch selects the fixed OrderID 2.
The correlated count asks how many order lines match when the predicate only needs to know whether one exists.
Every order can assign @OrderID. The final value is unspecified for multiple rows, and the previous value survives if there are none.
The insert into @OrderIds selects five unspecified orders.
No ordering determines which five orders populate #ImplicitOrders.
SELECT INTO infers the schema of #ImplicitOrders from the projection rather than declaring it explicitly.
The procedure declares and opens a cursor for up to two orders but fetches only one OrderID before closing it.
Concatenating the converted CustomerID produces different SQL text for different customers; a NULL CustomerID can also make the batch NULL.
EXEC runs the assembled customer lookup without binding CustomerID as an int parameter.
The order lookup embeds the converted @OrderID in the SQL text instead of using a parameter placeholder.
sys.sp_executesql receives only @Sql, with no parameter definition or bound OrderID.
#Scratch is explicitly created, never used, and left allocated until the procedure exits.
The handler returns ERROR_MESSAGE() as a result set and continues without signaling failure.
The negative OrderID path uses RAISERROR rather than THROW; RAISERROR does not honor XACT_ABORT.
PRINT emits a buffered diagnostic that is not a structured result or error.
The query always selects customer 1 instead of using the procedure's @CustomerID.
The order cutoff '20160101' is embedded in the predicate without a named business meaning.
Without a conversion style, '01/02/2016' can mean January 2 or February 1 depending on DATEFORMAT.
TOP (1) returns an unspecified order from the customer-matched invoice pairs.
COALESCE(o.CustomerID, 0) wraps the indexed Orders join key even though it is NOT NULL.
COALESCE(i.CustomerID, 0) also wraps the indexed Invoices join key even though it is NOT NULL.
The self-join returns one OrderID without defining which order to choose.
Joining Orders to itself on its primary key adds no filtering or columns to the result.
Sorting all orders by nvarchar(max) Comments can require substantial memory and tempdb space.
SUM(Quantity) covers all of Sales.OrderLines with no restriction on the orders included.
OrderID > 0 tests only the grouping key and can be expressed as a WHERE predicate before grouping.
COUNT(*) requests an exact count across all Sales.Orders rows.
COUNT(*) without GROUP BY returns one row, so ordering by OrderCount has no effect.
MERGE adds unnecessary matching complexity when the only action is a matched update.
The matched action assigns target.Comments to itself and can fire update triggers without changing the value.
SET Comments = Comments can acquire write locks and fire update triggers without changing the order.
Deleting by Quantity alone removes every matching line across all orders, not a specific OrderLineID.
The delete treats -1 as a special quantity without naming its business meaning.
WAITFOR DELAY keeps the request waiting for one second while doing no work.
BEGIN TRANSACTION is outside a TRY/CATCH boundary that could handle a failure before the rollback.
The supplied Sales.Orders definition has no IDENTITY column, so enabling IDENTITY_INSERT fails when this branch runs.
EXEC sp_who leaves the system procedure's sys schema implicit.
SET ROWCOUNT 1 is not reset before later queries and writes, including the insert that should stage matching customers.
The category insert maps its two values by physical column order rather than naming CategoryID and CategoryName.
The staged category is assigned the fixed business identifier 99.
The customer insert relies on all four projected columns matching the destination table's column order.
The leading % prevents a prefix seek on the unique CustomerName index.
@CustomerName is concatenated into a quoted SQL pattern. Its contents can alter the executable batch instead of remaining search data.
sp_executesql runs the customer search with no parameter definition or bound search value.
The call names sp_executesql without its sys schema.
Every staged customer is eligible for recategorization; the active ROWCOUNT limit is not a customer-selection predicate.
The update assigns category ID 1 rather than deriving the intended category from the supplied value.
The OrderDate predicate rejects NULL-extended order rows, so customers without qualifying orders disappear from the LEFT JOIN.
The order filter fixes its cutoff at '2016-01-01' without a named parameter or explanation.
DeliveryMethodID = NULL is not a null test. DeliveryMethodID is also declared NOT NULL, so no customer can satisfy the intended condition.
dbo.GetCustomerType(CustomerID) can require a scalar function invocation per customer unless SQL Server can inline it.
An error after BEGIN TRANSACTION can leave the transaction open or uncommittable because this handler never rolls it back.
The handler selects ERROR_MESSAGE() and continues, so callers need not receive an error when the transactional delete fails.
INDEX = 1 forces clustered-index access rather than letting SQL Server consider the unique CustomerName index for the LIKE predicate.
The first derived table starts three nested layers that merely pass CustomerID through from the innermost query.
LIKE '%A%' requires searching within CustomerName rather than seeking a prefix in its index.
SELECT * exposes every column returned by GetCustomerOrdersMulti and couples the result shape to the function definition.
GetCustomerOrdersMulti appears to be a multi-statement TVF. If confirmed by its definition, an inline equivalent could expose its query to the optimizer.
